                                           I.       INTRODUCTION

           The New Mexico Large Customer Group (“NMLCG”) submits this Initial Post-Hearing

Brief in support of the Comprehensive Stipulation (“Stipulation”).1 The Stipulation allows

Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS” or the “Company”) to provide safe and reliable

service, establishes important New Mexico customer protections, and mitigates rate impacts to

customers. It is in the public interest and should be approved in its entirety. Below, the NMLCG

first supports the Stipulation before addressing the Hearing Examiners’ (“HE”) Production Tax

Credit (“PTC”) related questions.

                     II.     LEGAL STANDARD REGARDING STIPULATIONS

           The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“Commission” or “NMPRC”) “has a

well-established policy encouraging the filing of stipulations, and it has adopted rules governing

procedures to consider settlements negotiated by the parties.”2 The Commission adopts contested

stipulations “by, first, affording any non-stipulating party an opportunity to be heard on the merits

of the stipulation…and second, making an independent finding, supported by substantial evidence


1
    Comprehensive Stipulation (Jun. 22, 2026) (“Stipulation”).
2
    See Case No. 21-00269-UT, Certificate of Stipulation, pp. 20-21 (Oct. 12, 2022).


                                                           1
 in the record, that the stipulation does indeed resolve the matters in dispute in a way that is fair,

just and reasonable and in the public interest.”3 Notably, “strong public policy favor[s] the

settlement of disputes to avoid costly and protracted litigation and the recognition that a

cooperative approach may be more effective in reconciling the interest of all parties than would be

the polarization which often accompanies adversarial proceedings.”4

        Here, the Commission provided Commission Staff (“Staff”)—the only non-stipulating

party—an opportunity to be heard at the hearing on the merits. As set forth below, substantial

evidence in the record demonstrates the Stipulation is in the public interest. The Commission

should thus approve the Stipulation in its entirety.

                     III.    ARGUMENT IN SUPPORT OF STIPULATION

        The NMPRC must set rates that are “just and reasonable,” and avoid subjecting rate classes

“to any unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage.”5 The Commission, when it sets just and

reasonable rates, “balance[s] the [utility] investor’s interest against the ratepayer’s interest” and

prevents economic waste.6 The Stipulation strikes this balance.

        The Stipulation sets the Company’s revenue requirement and return on equity (“ROE”) at

the mid-point between the Company’s and stakeholders’ original positions, ultimately reducing

the Company’s requested revenue requirement increase by approximately fifty percent.7               It

establishes a range of New Mexico customer protections, including (1) jurisdictional allocation

methodologies crediting New Mexico customers with resource capacity benefits 8; (2) Southwest

Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”) deficiency payment related guardrails9; and (3) reductions to Production

revenue allocation moves all classes closer to cost of service, and actually mitigates residential

customer rate increase more than Staff’s proposed methodology.11

        Only Staff opposes the Stipulation, largely because the stipulated revenue requirement is

“irreconcilable” with Staff’s recommended revenue requirement.12 But the Stipulation represents

a compromise, and appropriately “balance[s] the investor’s interest against the ratepayer’s

interest” in accordance with New Mexico precedent.13 Indeed, Stipulation signatories represent

utility, large customer, residential, and environmental interests. 14        As set forth below, the

Stipulation is in the public interest and should be adopted.

        A. The Stipulation revenue requirement is reasonable and falls within the range of
           the parties’ positions presented in the record.

        The Stipulation reduces SPS’s revenue deficiency from approximately $172.3 million to

$90 million—a nearly fifty percent decrease.15           This decrease is a product of good-faith

negotiation. The NMLCG originally recommended a $28.2 million revenue deficiency, 16 the

NMDOJ recommended a $109.8 million revenue deficiency,17 LES and FEA jointly recommended

a $120.99 million revenue deficiency,18 and Staff recommended a $47.7 million revenue

deficiency.19 The Stipulated revenue deficiency falls squarely within the range of the parties’

        The Stipulation revenue requirement incorporates a ROE of 9.50 percent, continuing the

level approved in SPS’s last rate case and again representing a reasonable compromise between

parties’ original positions.20 The Company originally requested a 10.50 percent ROE,21 the

NMLCG and OPL jointly recommended an 8.1 percent ROE,22 the NMDOJ recommended an 8.77

percent ROE,23 LES and FEA jointly recommended a 9.45 percent ROE,24 and Staff recommended

a 9.75 percent ROE.25 The Stipulated ROE falls within the parties’ original positions. Moreover,

as Staff noted, the Commission recently authorized SPS resource costs totaling $9 billion. 26 It is

critical that the Commission adopt the Stipulation, set the 9.50 percent ROE, and insulate New

Mexico ratepayers from excessive returns as the Company places the authorized resources in rate

base going forward.

        B. The Stipulation provides New Mexico ratepayers with key policy and ratemaking
           protections.

        The Stipulation also adopts critical ratepayer protections. It addresses Commission and

ratepayer concerns—raised here and in other SPS proceedings—regarding jurisdictional

allocation,27 expanding the Fuel & Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause (“FPPCAC”),28 SPP

below.

                1. The Stipulation ensures the Company credits New Mexico customers with
                   SPS resource capacity benefits.

         The Company originally failed to adjust its jurisdictional allocation methodology to credit

New Mexico customers with directly assigned resource capacity.31 The Commission previously

addressed this issue in Docket No. 25-00066-UT, finding it “is not just and reasonable to direct all

costs to New Mexico customers and then deprive those customers of the credit for the system wide

capacity benefit that that facility is providing.”32 The Commission directed SPS, in a future rate

case, to credit New Mexico customers with directly assigned resource capacity accordingly. 33

         The Stipulation meets this directive. It adjusts the Company’s jurisdictional allocation

methodology to credit New Mexico customers with all of the Cunningham Battery Energy Storage

System (“BESS”) capacity.34 The Company, moreover, committed to evaluate “the treatment of

directly assigned resources and the jurisdictional allocation of divergent state resource portfolios

for future proceedings.”35 This outcome protects New Mexico ratepayers on an immediate basis,

as it precludes SPS from charging New Mexico ratepayers twice for Cunningham BESS capacity. 36

And it represents a critical ratepayer protection going forward as the Company directly assigns

resources to New Mexico for Energy Transition Act compliance.

                 2. The Stipulation preserves the FPPCAC’s limited scope.

        SPS originally proposed to recover certain BESS Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA”)

capacity costs and SPP deficiency payments through the FPPCAC. 37 NMLCG challenged SPS’s

proposal to expand the FPPCAC here and in Case No. 25-00085-UT, where the Company similarly

requested to recover BESS PPA capacity costs through the FPPCAC. 38 Indeed, the FPPCAC is

limited in scope, designed to recover variable and market-based energy costs.39

        The Stipulation addresses these concerns.40 SPS agreed to withdraw its request to recover

BESS capacity costs through the FPPCAC, protecting New Mexico customers from an expanded

FPPCAC and resulting costs.41

                3. The Stipulation imposes guardrails related to SPP costs and benefits.

        The Company originally requested authority to (1) recover SPP deficiency payments from

New Mexico ratepayers; and (2) retain 10 percent of off-system SPP sales.42 Both proposals are

detrimental outcomes for New Mexico ratepayers.

        First, New Mexico statute and SPP protocols require SPS to secure sufficient capacity to

meet resource adequacy needs.43          The Company bears responsibility for related financial

repercussions—not New Mexico ratepayers. Second, off-system SPP sales reflect routine system

operations and resource management functions.44 The Company failed to demonstrate why the

Commission should reward shareholders for these functions at the expense of New Mexico

payment and off-system sales proposals and protecting ratepayers from related costs. 46

                 4. The Stipulation insulates ratepayers from excessive PTC-related returns.

        The Company originally requested a return on the PTC related DTA at the Company’s

weighted average cost of capital.47 The DTA here represents PTCs the Company (1) credited to

customers; but (2) has not utilized or transferred for revenue.48 Due to this timing mismatch, the

Company presumably accrues the PTC-related DTA at significant levels, entitling the Company

to significant returns. Indeed, the Company acknowledged its PTC “backlog” at hearing. 49 But

the Company failed to demonstrate the temporary timing mismatch justifies a full return at

ratepayers’ expense.50 The Stipulation mitigates the DTA returns, setting the return equal to the

Company’s cost of long-term debt.51                 This term, coupled with the NMLCG’s DTA

recommendation below, protects customers as the Company continues to generate PTCs and

accrue the DTA at greater levels.

        C. The Stipulation’s revenue allocation reflects SPS’s cost of service, is equitable, and
           mitigates residential rate impact.

        The Commission, when setting revenue allocation, considers “cost of service contribution,

continuity, stability, and gradualism in avoidance of rate shock.” 52 The New Mexico Supreme

Court determined revenue allocations that “support a more gradual movement towards each class

principle.

                 1. The Stipulation mitigates residential class rate increases with commercial
                    and industrial class subsidies.

        The Stipulation’s revenue allocation brings all rate classes closer to their cost of service—

but mitigates residential rate increases to a far greater extent than both the Company’s Class Cost

of Service Study (“CCOSS”) and Staff’s recommended revenue allocation.54 Indeed, SPS’s as-

filed CCOSS assigned the residential rate class a rate increase totaling 237.7 percent of the system

average rate increase.55 Staff’s proposed revenue allocation, in turn, assigned the residential rate

class a rate increase totaling 164.5 percent of the system average rate increase. 56 The Stipulation

appropriately moves the residential rate class closer to its cost of service, but to avoid rate shock,

reduces the residential rate increase to 139.5 percent of the system average rate increase.57

        The rate mitigation provided to the residential customer class is largely subsidized by the

commercial and industrial rate classes. The Stipulation assigns commercial and industrial classes

a rate increase at 89 percent of the system average—far greater than SPS’s CCOSS, which assigned

these classes a rate increase of approximately 61.6 percent of the system average increase.58

        Staff challenges the Stipulation revenue allocation, arguing the residential and small

customer classes’ base rate increases are too high. 59 But Staff relies on the wrong metric. It

                               IV.      RESPONSE TO HE QUESTIONS

         The HEs requested that parties address two PTC related concerns.64 First, the HEs

requested a “recommended methodology to ensure that [PTCs] accrued in a [DTA] by SPS do not

carry forward for an unreasonable amount of time.”65 Second, the HEs requested an explanation

regarding “why or why not…the ‘Energy-at-Source’ allocation of the PTCs provides a fair

allocation of the PTCs to the different rate classes on SPS’s system.” 66 The questions are addressed

in turn below.

         A. The Commission should limit PTC accrual to mitigate undue DTA returns.

         As set forth above, the Stipulation authorizes a return on the DTA at SPS’s cost of long-

term-debt—so long as the PTCs “remain unused or not yet transferred.”67 But the Stipulation does

not limit how long the Company may carry forward PTCs through the DTA. Thus, the Company

could theoretically refrain from transferring or utilizing the PTCs, entitling the Company to

perpetual PTC returns through the DTA.

        The Commission should establish a reasonable limitation on the Company’s ability to carry

forward PTCs, ultimately mitigating undue DTA returns. Specifically, the Commission should

only authorize a return on the DTA for the period between:

   1. The date that SPS credits the PTC benefit to customers; and

   2. The earliest date SPS actually monetizes the PTC or, acting prudently, reasonably could

       have monetized it.

Below are proposed criteria dictating when SPS (1) monetizes PTCs and (2) could have reasonably

monetized PTCs.

               1. The Commission should consider PTCs “monetized” when SPS secures
                  PTC benefits.

       The PTC carrying charge methodology should specify when the Company “monetizes”

PTCs under both PTC direct utilization and PTC transfer mechanisms. First, if the Company

applies PTCs to directly reduce tax liability, the PTC should be “monetized” on the first date the

PTC reduces or reasonably could have reduced: (1) a quarterly federal estimated tax payment; (2)

an annual federal tax payment or other federal tax obligation; or (3) a payment or settlement

obligation under the consolidated group tax allocation agreement. Second, when the Company

transfers PTCs to an unrelated taxpayer, the PTC should be “monetized” on the date SPS receives

the transfer proceeds. But the Commission should prohibit carrying charges associated with SPS-

caused transfer delays, including failure to pursue a timely and prudent transfer.

               2. The Commission should preclude returns on PTCs that the Company
                  failed to monetize within 365 days after the Company originally generated
                  the PTC.

       The PTC carrying charge methodology should prohibit the Company from earning a return

on PTCs—included in the DTA—365 days after the Company generated the PTC. The Company

previously stated “180 days…is the average estimated time that SPS expects to sell the PTCs after



                                                11
 generation.”68 The 180-day benchmark similarly represents a reasonable timeframe for SPS to

earn a return on PTCs in the DTA. If SPS expects to monetize a PTC within 180 days, it should

not receive a return on PTCs—at the expense of ratepayers—exceeding this timeframe.

Nevertheless, 365 days represents a compromise. Ultimately, this limitation still provides an

incentive for the Company to monetize PTCs, and thus mitigate PTC related DTA returns, to

customers’ benefit.69

       B. The Energy-at-Source PTC allocator is a reasonable means of allocating PTC
          benefits among rate classes.

       The Stipulation allocates production and transmission costs—including costs associated

with resources generating PTCs—on an average-and-excess demand four-coincident-peak basis

but allocates PTCs on an energy basis.70 The PTC allocation method is a compromise, and in the

context of the Stipulation as a whole, represents a reasonable outcome despite customer classes’

varying per-kilowatt hour (“kWh”) rates.

       First, the Company earns PTCs consistent with electricity produced on a per-kWh basis.

The Stipulation reasonably allocates PTCs consistent with this energy-based characteristic.

Second, customer classes’ varying per-kWh rates reflect revenue allocation, rate design, and class

characteristics, and are thus irrelevant for PTC allocation purposes. For example, classes without

separate demand charges recover some demand-related costs through volumetric energy charges.

Classes with lower load factors, moreover, may have a higher average per-kWh rate because their

fixed and demand-related costs are spread over fewer kWh. The Energy-at-Source allocator, in

                                      V.      CONCLUSION

        The Stipulation represents a reasonable compromise, establishes ratepayer protections, and

mitigates rate impact. Thus, the NMLCG respectfully requests that the Commission approve the

Stipulation in its entirety.



Respectfully submitted August 14, 2026.
